parts.title: Hon. Dr. Jean Nepo Abdallah Utumatwishima

segments.text: Distinguished guests, leaders from government, industry, academia, and civil society, young innovators, and future scientists, ladies and gentlemen, good morning. It is an honor to join you today at this important conference on nuclear energy and scientific innovation.

I was very impressed by the energy the MC brought in the room, and I had prepared a motivational speech, but now I'm going to share with you a story. Maybe it will motivate you or it will make you angry. I don't know what's gonna happen.
So I will spare you the speech that I have prepared because the emcee has done the work. So my story is that I have been humbled by science. In 2017, I left Kigali to the United States of America .

I went to the National Institutes of Health in Bethesda, Maryland, to conduct my postdoc fellowship. I was placed in an institute called NIDDK, the National Institutes of Diabetes, Digestive and Kidney Disease. So I was about to study diabetes epidemiology, but mainly I was in a lab where we were investigating the cardiometabolic risk factors for African immigrants in the greater metropolitan area of Washington.

So we were looking for the reasons why we Africans in sub-Saharan Africa get diabetes, type two diabetes, hypertension at an early age. So that was what we were investigating in my lab. But because when I was here, my job was I was doing some surgery and I was doing some thyroid surgery, you know, thyroid cancer surgeries.

I used to do some thyroid surgeries, goiters, and my process was simple. I, you know, you do the surgery with your hands, you open, you know, the neck, you identify with my own eyes, the recurrent nerve, and you remove the tumor, you send the tumor for pathology, and then they tell you it's a cancer, it's benign, it's malignant, then you start maybe some treatments. But when I went for the grand rounds of surgical endocrinology, I found this sophisticated machine and they called it PET scan.

And I was like, what is that? They said, they told me, you told us that you were doing surgery in Africa, and I said, yes. And I removed the tumor and I would locate recurrent nerve and I would send the tumor to pathology. And then you guys, you are even showing me some other areas, they would show me the tumor in the neck, some active areas in the nodes.

And I was like, this is new. So I tried to imagine myself, this PET scan identified some metastases far from the, you know, the area, the neck where we're operating. So I remember that I was telling my team back home that probably they are patients we didn't treat well because we didn't have PET scan.

I'm glad that PET scan has now arrived in Kigali. And I want to commend this nuclear science conference and the understanding that these young people should understand that we wanted this nuclear energy as of yesterday. So we need to go there and we need to do that as quickly as possible.
I thank you very much. Thank you.

Ladies and gentlemen, please a round of applause for Miss from the women in Amanda Mbhele is a nuclear young generation as well as Mr Johnson Lorlornyo Abusah from the Ghana young generation Network. Yes.

I love the energy more clapping so Amanda and Johnson will be sharing with us today how they got into the nuclear sector. Please listen. Thank you Hello Good morning and I would like to give an opportunity to my Counterpart for an introduction as well. Probably Thank you very much. Currently here in Africa we produce about 30% of the global critical minerals and of these but not limited to Cobalt we produce 76% of the global supply.

There is also manganese we produce 66% there is also chromium 46% and the whooping 80% of Plutonium sorry platinum However, these are the materials that are needed for the production of green technology and this green technology Involved electric vehicles. We are looking at battery storage systems as well as you know solar panels. So basically we have the resources but according to the World Economic Forum in 2025 Africa captures less than 1% of the total economic value Generated in green technology. So we have the resources for the technology but we are not able to process them.

So we ship them out of the country. They get processed and sold back to us at a premium. So clearly we do not have a resource challenge We have a processing challenge and for us to process our minerals We need reliable stable electricity and that is where nuclear Technology comes in and the good news is that Recently in 2025 the World Bank actually lifted a ban on sponsoring nuclear power plants So now there is funding to Africa sits on 20% of the global uranium reserve so we have the resources for the nuclear power plants to fuel them and also 34 African countries are signatory to a pact that they want to increase the they want to triple the Nuclear capacity by 2050 of which seven African countries are part South Africa, Ghana and then Rwanda who are hosted Are also part of that signatory. So we have the resources.

We have the technology and we have the government support Now what is left is the most critical part The human resource and that is where we the youth comes in so it is my belief That the youth are the next Generation to lead the energy transition in Africa and for us to do that We will need the support of all the stakeholders involved So what we need from our stakeholders invited invited here humbly is that we want support for expertise Training of which I am a beneficiary decaf from my His excellency, mr. Wood is here supporting us to do that and I was a beneficiary of the atomic energy scholarship in China. Which is sponsored by the Chinese? National nuclear corporation, so I'm grateful to them as well and I have my professor professor I don't worry about who is currently the DG of the Ghana Atomic Energy Commission. He helped me during my master's So we have all these and we hope that more of these will be done for the youth and secondly for the youth Organizations that are pushing at the forefront of pushing the agenda to have the youth included in such discussions We we believe that we have support for them to also expand their Reach, for example, we met as a member from South Sudan What do they know that there's something like a young generation nuclear but because of us he's happy to go and propagate the same message in this country and we hope that it would it would energize the youth in the country and Finally to the youth that are present here I know that it is our dream that after the training we get opportunities But then I believe we are not limited to just what we are taught for me I did data science in nuclear engineering But now I am a data scientist because currently I have not been transitioned into the nuclear industry yet So that is what I am keeping by so I believe this is also an important factor that we the youth need to look at so we don't solely depend on the Stakeholders or the organizations that are in our countries we can build something for ourselves since we are the The next leadership and for this I would say that I hope and pray That in the next decades to come there will be a proliferation of nuclear power plants across the continent in Africa having engineers who are Africans trained in Africa operating African nuclear power plants generating energy Generating energy to process our raw materials so we can get the benefit from it so on this note, I would say that we the youth are the next generation of Leading the nuclear transition in Africa. Thank you.

Thank you so much for that. And indeed you are The leaders as it is so I'd like to I was brought here as an Inspiration I'd say and I would like to I'm so happy to see young people in uniforms particularly because that's where I started as well and so I'm gonna share my journey with you and I'm pleased to be part of the 60% of the youth of Africa and I'm proud to be there. So where do I come from? I come from South Africa from a small township of Umlazi and that's where I did my high school and The school was in township, if you know the history of South Africa I understand that townships were basically congested areas with that were meant for black people during the Apartheid so I come from that and the school that I went to was Okwini Interestingly enough that Okwini used to not have met in science before but it became the first black school in South Africa To have met in science in other technical subjects in 1985.

So I then later joined in my young years And started doing maths and science and thanks to the democracy the new government that time and After that, I moved to do my engineering my engineering and environmental geology at the University of Brazil Natal So I am Zulu indeed and How did I then become a person of nuclear during my undergrad studies? I was doing geology. So we did a lot of Paleontology geophysics and one interesting part about geophysics that will also use the date water young water like myself and in aquifers. But it also dates fossils, one of the fossils that is famous in South Africa. It's Mrs. Pless and that was found just outside Johannesburg and Mrs. Pless was used to that was dated using carbon-14 and the water we used to date here water using tritium So this was my mini introduction into nuclear but it was not sufficient because I did not connect it to the entire industry of the country fast forward I graduated and then I went to a conference similar to this and I met a people of Nexa and there I was intrigued to see radioactive waste and I was curious because now I saw that they putting these things underground which the disposing of I was curious that they're gonna Probably contaminate the aquifer, but which is not the case So I wanted to learn more how do they ensure safety and I interacted with the group at that time and fortunately enough You have a chance to interact with them because they currently at the exhibition stand.

It's exactly the same people. I met in 2014 and It was from that that sparked Inspiration inside of me and then I went into Doing more research and they actually absorbed me as a volunteer So when I had people talking about philanthropy, I was like I was I joined nuclear as a philanthropist so they joined that I joined NEXA as a volunteer and a government agency and I Started learning more about nuclear and I got very much interested So I thought I should transition from just being a geologist but to being a nuclear Engineer with geology and just focus on the back end so that I ensure that we safely dispose All our waste in the in the country and Fortunately after I had joined I did a lot of science communication So I'm used to talking to young people and encouraging them into Getting into STEM subjects, but also telling them about nuclear at large and I do that as it's sort of like Yeah, it's a philanthropy work. I'd say I Then had a privilege to go to South Korea to study nuclear engineering after that and I made it in radioactive waste management and decommissioning So after having done that I had a privilege again to join the IEA as a spent fuel management project assistant Which exposed me to various ICRPs I had an opportunity to review a number of papers and which then brings me to say Knowledge is power because it was at that point where I even going more global experience when it comes to nuclear I then got back.

I was like, oh, I don't want to be out in the country I want to go back and plow in my own country So I decided to go back to South Africa, which the minister advised that you can go study abroad But please come back and give back to the community So I did exactly that I went back to my country and I wanted to be involved in projects that we were key projects in managing spent fuel in the country and I was part of that project and I had led I've led decommissioning projects within the institutions as well and Thereafter I Thereafter I went to work for Rosatom. But before I even went to Rosatom, I want to bring something that happened in 2023 it's I had an opportunity to to experience the Declaration that happened at COP 28. So since I said I'm a philanthropist, so I do a lot of UN climate change UN Cooperation of parties conferences whereby I go there to advocate for nuclear as a clean source and a green source that can contribute to the Agendas that you have agenda 23 of Africa, but also the agenda of 2050 So the declaration of tripling nuclear by 2050 I was there and I was proud at that moment It was only Ghana that was on stage a out of all African countries And I was hoping that oh I hope as we move more African countries join and last year this year actually our president our Minister as well declared it endorsed to the declaration So it's such movements that keep us inspired and but to the young people I want to say One thing I've learned as well through my journey I went to Rosatom and then now I'm working for the disposal facility within my country again And I'm part of various groups young groups the a YGN the wind global young generation I'm also a president of my chapter of my organizational chapter in my company for Windsor is that you have to be resilient because challenges will come and challenges in form of In non-human challenges, but also human challenges.

So you just have to keep to your dream as Alex said keeps your dream and focus on it Do not lose sight but also be proactive make sure that you put yourself out there make sure that you use internet Because we're in the age of internet use internet to find such places where you can interact network and expand yourself because knowledge is power and we were mentioning this yesterday that People fear what they don't know. I've always also preached that when I was a science communicator people fear what they don't know. So Knowledge is power put yourself out there learn as much as you can and you will see that the globe will be or is your world is your oyster and Maybe to even give you a bit of encouragement nuclear is global as a result of travel to more than 30 countries And this is me taking leave to just go and train myself attend trainings attend put myself out there attend webinars attend Discussions just on my own because I want to be out there and I am passionate about science communication and putting nuclear I was there.
Thank you so much Thank you
Please may welcome our moderator for the session, Queenter Osoro , a nuclear scientist from the Nuclear Power and Energy Agency. We have as the panelists,Bianca Carpinelli
Coordination Officer, IAEA,Mervyn Fischer
Chief Executive Officer (CEO), Allweld Nuclear & Industrial
Dr. Francesca Giovannini
Executive Director, Harvard Kennedy School - Belfer Center
Karen Hallberg
Secretary General, Pugwash Conferences on Science and World Affairs
And.Dr.Tracey-Ann Wellington
Deputy Head of the Office of Policy and Coordination, OECD NEA
Thank you so much, Alexis, for the introduction. My name is Queenter Osoro , as I've been told. I'm going to be the moderator for this session.

So this session is for the youth, and I'm happy to see that we have the young generation with us, and they are going to be very conversational, and I expect that you will learn more from our panelists. So the panel that is in front of us, first of all, we'd like to thank you for accepting to share with us your expertise, and we believe that from your very much experience, our youth are going to take one or two from you. So I have my panelists from the industry, that is the training.

I have from the International Atomic Agency, that is the policies, and we also have from academia, the training, and also OECD. So welcome to the session. So we have all the five panelists here, and we have Bianca from the IAEA.

We have Marvin, with the CEOs of Allied Nuclear and Industrial. Dr. Francisca, who is previously here as the moderator, is the Executive Director and Project on Managing Atom, that is the Harvard Kennedy School, Belfer Center. And then we also have Karen, Dr. Tracey, and welcome to this panel.

So I'd like to ask a quick question that I expect all of you to weigh in, and this is just mostly to tell our youth, we've talked about they have to be out there, they have to do the work. But now, let me ask our panelists, what does it mean to work in the nuclear sector? And what are some of the capacities that they have to build to make them very resourceful, and also include their expertise to be part of the nuclear sector? So I'll start with Tracey. Thank you very much.

So when I think of what it takes to work in the nuclear sector, in my mind, it's not limiting yourself. How I started out, I got into nuclear because I, in my PhD program, needed an extra class to have a full schedule, and somebody said, why not take a nuclear class? I'd never done nuclear before, this is a PhD program, that's not the time in which you find something new to do. But I joined the class, found it very interesting, and changed my entire education path, career path going forward.

And so I think what it takes to be in nuclear, and I don't think this is limited to nuclear, is to be open to opportunities. I noticed Amanda mentioned earlier, doing your research, looking into opportunities that are in there, and taking the initiative to take your career forward. Thank you very much.

I am very honored to be able to represent Harvard University. I just want to say one minute about Harvard, because I care, especially at this moment in time, to say it. If you're sitting there thinking Harvard University is just a white, dude-privileged university, you'll be wrong.

Harvard made its name because we are deeply international. And in fact, my school, the Harvard Kennedy School, 62% of the students are international. If you want to be the number one university in the world, you have to find talent where it is.

And it's not only in the United States, and it's not only white, and it's not only male. And to the young women in particular, in the audience, this is directed to you. What does it take to work in nuclear? I see some sitting in the audience, like Ambassador Laura Holgate and others who have made a very big career in this field.
For women, the threshold is higher. You cannot wing it. You cannot improvise.

You have to know your stuff. Because this is a field, unfortunately, still very much dominated by men and by technical people. And so if you work in policy, if you are interested in being a negotiator for a legal agreement, if you want to work for a nuclear supplier, or if you work for a think tank that wants to provide strategic thinking to a government, but you are a woman, you need to know the language, you need to know your expertise very, very well.
So professionalism in this field is a must. Because it's a small field, everyone knows you. Reputation costs, if you actually lack professionalism, are very, very high.
So my number one advice is know your stuff and be confident about how much you know. Thank you, Francesca. That was really, really to the point.

And I don't want to be repetitive in that sense. What I just want to highlight is how it feels to work in the nuclear energy space right now? Well, it's pretty exciting. We are living exciting moments right now.

We've seen that this week. In the hype case projection, the IAEA foresees that nuclear energy in Africa will triple by 2030 and will increase tenfold by 2050. That will open a huge window of opportunity for the new workforce to come in.
So if you want to shape the next generation of the energy landscape in Africa, that will include nuclear. And you just need to get on board. Okay, good morning, everyone.
So I think my message to the youth would be, it's not important where you come from. It's more important where you're going. And nuclear certainly provides you that.

So we heard Amanda's story. My story is pretty similar from a poor community to sitting today, being 30 years involved in the nuclear industry. And that's because there was a nuclear power station in the city that I grew up in.

And so we are hoping that for most of Africa, that we have that and that we can have the youth to have those opportunities. And then I would just add again, what my colleague said is you need to be resilient. Thank you.
Thank you. Good morning, everyone. My name is Karin Holberg.
I'm from Argentina. And in many aspects, I feel that we have a lot in common. So I'm very pleased to be here.

I thank the organizers for the invitation. I want to transmit a very short experience from my particular life of growing in a developing country that also had started with nuclear energy from the 50s, but took a very important decision to develop nuclear energy using their own technology and education. So I studied physics in Argentina, in the South of Argentina.

And this is where I met a professor who was so interesting because we would get engaged in discussions, not only about, he was teaching me nuclear physics, but not only about nuclear physics, but also about the applications, about the social implications, about the responsibility of scientists in what we do. So when I finished my PhD, I also got to know about the Pugwash Conferences, which is where I'm the secretary general now, at the Pugwash Conference. Pugwash is the name of a Canadian town where the first meeting was held.

And this was created by Albert Einstein and Bertrand Russell, another very prominent scientist, in 1957. So a long time ago, but when the H-bomb, the thermonuclear bomb was being developed because scientists had to get together to discuss the consequences of their research. So the dual use, to do research for positive and for wellbeing, the welfare of humanity, and try to discuss the potential misuses of science.

And this is why, together, in parallel with my career, and I'm saying this on purpose because I'm talking to people who are young, people of you that want to decide whether to continue a technical career like engineering, physics, biology, or a social career, political science, science, et cetera. I did my parallel career in Pugwash and learned about diplomacy and scientific diplomacy. So this is a very interesting path forward you have if you get engaged in nuclear, for example, in nuclear technologies, but it also has consequences in other technologies.

Last year, I was in Ghana, my first time in Sub-Saharan Africa. And I was amazed to see the young people there because I was a judge in a quantathon. They were coding a quantum computer based in Switzerland and they were so motivated and they had a very good training.

So this really gives me hope that you are the future and the present, not only the future. Thank you so much. What is coming out clearly is that as a youth, when you want to join the nuclear field or want to get involved with nuclear, what is important is curiosity.

Also, you have to get to do the work. Like you have to increase your curiosity in terms of developing your expertise. And also something coming out clearly is that nuclear is a multidisciplinary sector.

We don't have to be scientists, we don't have to be engineers. We need finance, we need IT, we need all the technical expertise and even the social bit of it, we need communicators in nuclear. So that is what I would add to the youth.

Don't look at it like, if I'm not a scientist, I'm not an engineer, I cannot join the nuclear sector. All disciplinary expertise are welcomed in nuclear and they can develop in various capacities. Thank you.

So, building onto that, our first question will go to Bianca from the IAEA. We know that the IAEA is now helping member states to develop their capacity in various areas. So I would like to know, what are some of the experience, from your experience from IAEA in your own perspective, what are some of the international mechanisms that the IAEA has used that you've seen work in terms of best practices to help member states develop their capacity and also to build their capacity in terms of legal, technical expertise and so on? Thank you very much.

I will answer that question maybe a bit more in practical terms on some initiatives that we are having in the nuclear space for promoting women into getting into the nuclear sector. And these are two flagship initiatives, the Madis-Klodowska-Kudy Fellowship Program and the Lisa Minor Program. The first one, the Madis-Kudy Fellowship Program, promotes and supports young women to get into the studies of nuclear energy by supporting them with their master's studies and then offering them a very exciting opportunity of having an internship in the IAEA.

So that's one side of the coin. And then the Lisa Minor Program that is targeted to mid-career women as well, provide leadership training, mentorship and access to facilities and site visits to help them grow in their mid-careers and so forth. These two initiatives are open for women from all member states of the IAEA, of course, including African countries.

So I really encourage the young women in the room that are interested in embarking on a nuclear career or fostering further skills and developing further knowledge on their nuclear journey to apply to Madis-Kudy or to Lisa Minor Program. So I invite you to get into our website, follow our social media and stay tuned when these new cycles of applications roll out. We are very proud about promoting these two flagship initiatives that DG Grossi has put forward specifically for women in the nuclear sector.

And then on also engaging and building further skills and capacity building, but also being really immersed into what's happening on the nuclear space and conversations. The IAEA hosts conferences around the year on all the different topics that we work on. So we're always happy to receive abstracts from the younger generation to participate in those and also to engage in the youth events that we have in different multilateral engagement opportunities, for example, in COPS.

I've seen some of them engaged in past opportunities. So that's already happening, but I invite you to also stay tuned to what we are doing in that space. And also we have a very broad internship program.

So stay tuned at the openings of vacancies for internship programs in the IAEA. Again, open to young people from all our member states. So I'm here and also my director Wei Wang that is around here is also here today at the conference.

We're always happy to answer more questions, provide you with advice and give you more information when you need. But please, I just want to amplify that we have so many opportunities for you for the young generation to, as I said, get on board this journey. So we don't want you to miss out on that.
Thank you so much, Bianca. I'm happy that you mentioned Lise Meitner. I have to say I'm the first baby of Lise Meitner.

I was in the first cohort. We were hosted at the North Carolina State University and those connections have gone far and far from the way 2023 when you joined. And I really thank the IAEA for that initiative because it has made us love a lot of connections.
Lisa Marshall was our host. So some of the initiatives given by the IAEA like she has mentioned. So women and the youth in the team, please take advantage of these opportunities.

They will always be there, but if you don't go for them, nobody will come for you. So building on that, I'd like to ask Mr. Mervyn, you're in the training academy that is the Allied Nuclear. So my question is in the workforce gap, some of these industry perspectives that you have, what are some of the skills and competencies that you find most lacking in today's emerging nuclear workforce as you work in your company? I think that the universities and technicians do a pretty good job at getting people ready for industry.
However, in the nuclear industry, there are some differences. And the most significant is safety culture, nuclear safety culture and human error prevention. So those are the main gaps.

And at Orwell Training Academy, those are the gaps we try to focus on because we're trying to get them ready for a workplace setting. So we also try to get them exposure to nuclear plants and that makes a difference to someone really touching the plant. Okay, okay, thank you so much, Mervyn.

So some of the gaps and some of the ways they are trying to break the gaps, Mervyn has explained. So on this professional development, we've talked about the IEA talking about how they're helping the youth, and then Mervyn has indicated some of the gaps that you see. Dr. Francisca, allow me to ask you, beyond the technical expertise, how important for the future nuclear professionals to understand diplomacy, international norms and global governance? That is, how do we take the conversation beyond just having the technical expertise? Well, thank you so much.

This is, I think, one of the most important questions. So let me say Harvard Kennedy School, part of the Harvard University family, our mandate is really to train the new generation of policymakers. So people who are recruited and come as students are expected most likely to serve in government, to serve in advisory roles, to serve in policy.

So designing norms, engaging with international organizations, leading, for example, frameworks in various multilateral agencies or domestic agencies. And I think it's important to say that when we train our students at Harvard Kennedy School, we fundamentally focus on three things, which go beyond the technical training, but can be applicable across the board. The first one is strategic thinking.

So if you are going to be serving as an advisor or as a leader in a nuclear institution, you most likely need to know who are the groups that have what interest. So understanding the interest that drive the conversation is key. So strategic thinking is really one of our skill development goals.

The second is negotiation, and really negotiation and diplomacy. You can have the best plan in the world, but if you don't know how to sell it, you're not going very far. And all policymakers need to be trained in understanding the trade-offs that they need to make between proposition A and proposition B. So we really try to train them on diplomacy.

And the third element is framing or communication, which you talked about. So the leaders of today and tomorrow need to know how to communicate to what audience. So again, you can be a technical person or you can be a policy person, but if you speak and nobody understands what you're saying, you're not going to go very far in the field.
And so these three elements cut across our technical degrees and our policy degrees. Harvard Kennedy School also has two levels. We have a master program.

In fact, one of you, especially one of Rwanda's talents, is actually with us. It's a two-year master program. You can specialize in public policy, in technology, in energy, in various other disciplines.

And you can also decide to tailor it towards nuclear. The graduate program allows you to engage also with a lot of policy skills development. That's why in between the two years, you will actually be sent to do an internship.

If you want to work in nuclear, most likely you will work in a nuclear supply, in a nuclear company or in a regulatory agency or in a domestic agency in the United States or a multilateral agency. The second layer, which I want to stress here, is the post-graduate level. Now, some of you will want to go straight into work, which is perfect.

But Harvard as a university also needs to ensure that the research and development in this field continues. And so for those of you who actually don't want necessarily to just work straight away, but you want to go for a post-graduate degree, we have a very large fellowship program called Managing the Atom Fellowship Program, which opens every October 1st for post-graduate students. So you are doing a PhD and you have a research proposal that you really want to develop, or you have just defended your thesis and you actually want to become a professor, but you want to have a gap here to work on a research project or a book project, then Harvard gives you the mentoring, the support, and quite frankly, the peer community to actually continue your research.
So we prepare both for the policy track, but also for the long-term research career. Thank you so much. And I like that she has mentioned the fact that you need to have to develop soft skills.

She talked about negotiation skills. So as much as you have the technical expertise, you also have to have a way of communicating and also even convincing. So some of these interactive skills are also very important in the nuclear field.

And the all-round nature of nuclear field brings me now to Karen. Karen, in the Pugos, you say that you bring together scientists, policy experts that shows it is very all-round. So I want you to explain to our youth the diverse career pathways.

Many young people associate nuclear careers primarily with technical roles. What opportunities exist to those who want to contribute through policy, ethics, diplomacy, or even international corporations? This is a very important question, and it's also building up on what Francesca was saying. We need technical expertise, but technical expertise means many different careers.
We already mentioned physics, engineering, biology, biomedics, technicians at these different levels. It doesn't have to be a high-level university degree. Mathematics, computer science …

I think I said it. Now, it's also, as we said, we need another expertise, which is communication skills in the nuclear field is very important because it is a very strong social dimension to nuclear energy. And that has to be well-managed.

It's very difficult as a scientist or as an engineer to transmit very technical issues like probabilities, radiation effects, et cetera. And people tend to be afraid of radiation. So for example, in medical physics, if you have research reactors, you have to explain to the patients what you're doing.

If there is a nuclear research reactor, people might be afraid because they're thinking of what happened in Chernobyl, what happened in Fukushima. So we need people who know how to communicate, but also know the technical aspects of that. That is a very subtle skill.

And then we need, for example, diplomats, people who are also working in other topics like policymakers. So I would like to say that for the technical people who have technical training, it's good for them to also know and have knowledge about international treaties, about regulations. This is important for a job in the nuclear field, about communication.

But let me go to the other side. If you look at, for example, policymakers or diplomats, it's also important for them to have a basic knowledge of what the technical aspects are. Then you put them together like we do in Pugwash, and they talk to each other.

They talk to each other mostly in closed rooms because they are not representing institutions. They're talking for themselves because of their own expertise. And then we use science not only for scientific knowledge, but we use it for scientific rationale, the way scientists discuss things in an open way, based on facts with critical thinking, acknowledging our own mistakes when the other person is using arguments to convince us.

So this is the scientific soft skill, which is a scientific rationale to discuss problems in a very difficult and a very complex world, which is a political world. Thank you so much, Karen. I think it's coming out clearly, and it's very common for all of us that we need these skills, we need the technical.

And Karen has said that we have the collaboration between the technical expertise and the ones who are in the soft skills. So building on this, I would like to ask Dr. Tracey, like we do from the OECD, where you help countries develop safe, economical and responsible use of nuclear energy. This is like a global village.
One time your DG said nuclear is a global village. Welcome to the village. So my question is, working with the OECD requires collaboration across governments, institutions and technical disciplines.

What key skills should young people develop to succeed in such international and multidisciplinary environments like the OECD? If you are young people who'd like to be like you, please tell them what to have. I think also Bianca could talk about this because of the international organization space. The interesting thing about it is it's very, it represents a lot of different countries, cultures and experiences, but it's not only regulated to that. I mean, Francesca mentioned Harvard and the 62% international population.
